title: UPDATED: Mental health boost called for in wake of Welton death
article: Better communication between police and mental health officials has been advised following an inquest into the death of Derek Welton.
The four-day B.C. Coroner's inquest into Welton's police-shooting death wrapped up with seven recommendations from the four-man, three woman jury.

"In this inquest into the death of Derek Wayne Welton it is our opinion that he could have been better served by the resources with in the province of British Columbia," the jury's foreman said before reading out the recommendations on Thursday.

"We recommend the RCMP review their training strategies in dealing with mental health situations," he continued. "This review should include the use of available psychiatric resources such as B.C. Mental Health and Addiction Services and the Forensic Psychiatric Services Commission. These resources are to be accessed when required at an incident."
The jury then recommended the North Cowichan/Duncan RCMP undertake a review of its tactical team strategies regarding incidents of this nature.
"We also recommend tactical decisions at the scene include entry and exit strategies (and) be discussed beforehand and wholly understood by all parties," the foreman continued.
RCMP Cpl. Darren Lagan said inquest recommendations are forwarded to the local detachment's commander, as well as the commanding officer for the division, for review.

"It's a tragic situation all around and it deserved the examination it had, and we will certainly examine the recommendations of the jury, and if we can implement them we will commit to doing that," he said on Tuesday.
Lagan said the recommendations are natural ones, and noted inquest findings often lead to changes in policing.
"It's an ever-evolving process and as society changes, so does the way we have to react as police officers," he explained.
The jury's recommendations, meanwhile, were also directed at public health officials.
The British Columbia Review Board was advised to notify local agencies such as the RCMP, mental health and the local hospital authorities when an absolute discharge is granted against medical advice.

And the Minister of Health was advised to conduct an extensive review of the resources currently available, due to the apparent lack of facilities for psychiatric patients in the province, and in particular in Cowichan.
"We will look closely at (the recommendations) and work with VIHA and other health authorities to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future," a statement from the ministry reads.

The jury also recommended the director of Duncan Mental Health develop a local outreach program, styled on the model in Victoria, and advised regular meetings between the RCMP and Duncan Mental Health. It also called for employing more than one forensic psychiatric nurse in the Cowichan Valley.

Kelly Reid, director of mental health and addictions services at VIHA, said the recommendations -- such as regular meetings with police and a more robust outreach program -- "make a great deal of sense."

"We know that Cowichan as an area within VIHA has less mental health and addiction services than Victoria or Nanaimo, for instance, and it's been flagged for more funding for a number of years," he said, adding VIHA has taken steps to address that with additions to mental health services at Caulfield Place and Cowichan Lodge.

"There's also increased funding in addiction services this year, so we plan to continue to help the Cowichan Valley catch up with bigger, urban areas like Nanaimo and Victoria in terms of per capita funding," Reid said.

"Our hearts really go out to the family and those involved in this situation. It's the worst-case scenario for the individual, the family and we just feel a great deal of sympathy -- and want to do everything possible to prevent this kind of outcome from happening again."
Derek Welton received two hits from a Taser and was shot twice on March 1, 2009, after RCMP arrived at his home in response to an abandoned 911 call.

Welton had taken illicit drugs that day and his calls to 911 indicated he was acting irrationally at the time. Welton had also been recently discharged -- against medical advice -- from the Lower Mainland's Forensic Psychiatric Hospital.
In fact, the inquest revealed a doctor had even written to local RCMP to warn them about Welton's return to town -- something Cowichan officers admitted was unusual.
Mounties at the scene had planned to apprehend Welton under the Mental Health Act and take him to hospital for treatment.
However, he tried to attack the officers with knives after the first shot from a Taser.
Cpl. Greg Pask fired his weapon three times that evening.
Welton was hit twice.
He continued to fight police afterward, which is when the Taser was used a second time.
Welton died at Cowichan District Hospital that evening. The inquest indicated the cause of death was a gunshot wound to the abdomen.

The Mounties involved have been cleared of any criminal wrongdoing after a lengthy police investigation. The coroner's inquest is standard procedure in a police-involved shooting, and aims to prevent future deaths in similar situations.
Welton's inquest was conducted by presiding coroner Rodrick MacKenzie and had recommendations for various agencies.
